# Mesh Assembly and Data Structure

Also called: Mesh Assembly, Chunk Mesh Assembly, Mesh Data Structures

## Overview
Mesh Assembly and Data Structure defines the in-memory representation, buffer allocation, and finalization of voxel geometry for GPU submission. It solves the problem of translating raw, exposed face data into contiguous, typed arrays (vertices, indices, normals, attributes) that can be efficiently consumed by graphics APIs. It sets itself apart from [Block face vertex layout](2374-block-face-vertex-layout.md) by focusing on the aggregation and packing of data rather than the geometric definition of individual quads, and from [Voxel Face and Geometry Generation](11724-voxel-face-and-geometry-generation.md) by handling the post-generation assembly and validation rather than the face culling logic itself.

## Shared principles
The family operates on the output of the geometry generation phase (exposed faces/sections). The core mechanism involves aggregating these sections into contiguous memory buffers organized by render layer or material.

1.  **Layer/Section Aggregation:** Geometry is grouped by render layer (e.g., Opaque, Water, Transparent) or material ID. Each group tracks its own `vertexOffset`, `vertexCount`, `indexOffset`, and `indexCount` within the global buffers [S2, 4100-chunk-mesh-assembly.md, unofficial].
2.  **Contiguous Buffer Allocation:** Arrays are pre-allocated based on the total quad count ($N_{quads}$) across all layers. This ensures cache-friendly access and minimal GPU memory fragmentation [S2, 4100-chunk-mesh-assembly.md, unofficial].
    *   Positions: $N_{quads} \times 4 \times 3$ floats.
    *   Normals: $N_{quads} \times 4 \times 3$ signed bytes (quantized).
    *   Indices: $N_{quads} \times 6$ unsigned integers.
    *   Attributes: $N_{quads} \times 4$ per attribute (e.g., `blockId`, `ao`, `lights`) [S2, 4100-chunk-mesh-assembly.md, unofficial].
3.  **Change Detection:** Assembly is skipped if the chunk has not changed (`HasChanges` is false), reusing the existing mesh to save CPU/GPU bandwidth [S1, 4100-chunk-mesh-assembly.md, unofficial].
4.  **Finalization:** The raw buffers are assigned to the mesh object, submeshes are defined, bounds are recalculated, and the mesh is attached to the renderer/collider components [S1, 4100-chunk-mesh-assembly.md, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Chunk Mesh Assembly](4100-chunk-mesh-assembly.md)
Aggregates mesh data from multiple render layers into contiguous typed arrays for efficient GPU submission. It solves the problem of fragmented geometry by consolidating vertices and indices from disparate voxel blocks into a single draw-call-friendly structure. Unlike [Block Render Data Structure & Instance Generation](6209-block-render-data-structure-instance-generation.md), which may rely on instancing or scattered buffers, this method packs all geometry into dense, contiguous memory regions, optimizing bandwidth and reducing draw call overhead.

### [Mesh Plugin Architecture](4921-mesh-plugin-architecture.md)
Provides an interface for pluggable meshing algorithms, allowing for extensibility within the geometry generation pipeline. It decouples the meshing logic from the chunk management system, enabling the selection of specific algorithms (e.g., blocky vs. smooth) based on voxel data types. This approach sets it apart from monolithic assembly methods by allowing runtime or configuration-time swapping of the meshing strategy without altering the underlying data structure or scheduling infrastructure.

### [Block Render Data Structure & Instance Generation](6209-block-render-data-structure-instance-generation.md)
Defines the in-memory representation of a single voxel block's rendering properties and generates the corresponding GPU draw instances. It solves the problem of efficiently passing per-face material and color data to the geometry shader or instance buffer without requiring complex vertex attribute layouts. It differs from [Chunk Mesh Assembly](4100-chunk-mesh-assembly.md) by focusing on the logical data container for a single block rather than the contiguous buffer allocation for a chunk, and from [Mesh Finalization](11478-mesh-finalization.md) by handling the initial creation and tint mixing rather than the final validation and bounding box computation.

### [Material-Based Mesh Sectioning](8778-material-based-mesh-sectioning.md)
Splits a decoded mesh into separate sections (arrays of triangles) based on the material ID associated with each triangle's vertices. It solves the problem of organizing geometry for GPU submission by grouping triangles that share the same material, enabling efficient batching and rendering. It differs from sibling methods like [Chunk Mesh Assembly](4100-chunk-mesh-assembly.md) by focusing on the logical disambiguation of material references rather than the geometric assembly or sectioning of the mesh itself.

### [Mesh Finalization](11478-mesh-finalization.md)
Prepares a raw geometric mesh for rendering by validating data integrity, computing derived attributes (normals, bounds), and organizing scalar/vector fields for efficient GPU access. It differs from [Mesh Assembly and Data Structure](6268-mesh-assembly-and-data-structure.md) by focusing on post-assembly validation and attribute computation rather than buffer allocation and vertex/index packing. It serves as the bridge between geometry generation and shader execution, ensuring that all required data structures are consistent and complete.

### Mesh Configuration and Data Structures
This variant specifies performance-critical data structure choices for JavaScript-based implementations. Block ID membership tests must use native JavaScript `Set` instead of custom `HashSet` implementations to avoid performance regressions (~400k tests per chunk) [S1, unofficial]. Block IDs must be registry-derived, converting untrusted numeric inputs via `BlockId.result` [S1, unofficial]. Transparent solids are split into two sets: `transparentSolidBlockIds` (glass, leaves) and `waterBlockIds` (dedicated shader) [S1, unofficial]. The `ChunkView` structure holds coordinates, height, and a byte view without implicit truncation [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The concepts originate from modern voxel game engines (e.g., Minecraft clones) and real-time terrain rendering systems. The specific data structures and assembly pipelines described are derived from implementations in [nerima-games/mc-meshing](https://github.com/nerima-games/mc-meshing) and related Unreal Engine/Unity voxel plugins [S1, 4100-chunk-mesh-assembly.md, unofficial]. The emphasis on contiguous buffers and change detection reflects optimizations for high-frequency updates in dynamic voxel worlds.
